title: The Well
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: The slow inheritance of a family secret
excerpt: The house was gone. He had known it would be gone; he had received the letter a year and a half ago. He had come, he told himself, only to see the field without the house on it. He was standing at the edge of the field before he admitted to himself, without words, that he had come to the well.

chapters.title: The Field
chapters.body:
The house was gone.

He had known it would be gone. He had received the letter from the county clerk a year and a half ago, informing him in careful bureaucratic language that the structure at the address on the tax rolls had been demolished after failing a series of safety inspections, that the parcel had been sold at auction to satisfy the outstanding lien, and that as the sole surviving grandchild he was entitled — if he wished, and if he could produce the requisite documentation — to a small portion of the proceeds of the sale, less fees. He had not wished. He had not produced any documentation. He had folded the letter twice and put it in the drawer where he kept things he did not know what to do with, and he had not thought of it again for some time.

He had, in fact, forgotten it completely, until a week ago. And now he was standing at the edge of the field where the house had been, in the last light of a Wednesday in September, and he was looking at nothing.

It was not entirely nothing. There was the field. There was the low stone wall along the road, from which a section had been removed to admit the trucks that had come with the demolition. There was the pale rectangle of raw earth where the foundation had been, only just beginning to green over. There was, at the far end of the rectangle, a slab of concrete that must have been the porch, and beside it a scatter of red brick from the chimney. But of the house itself there was nothing. The elm his grandfather had planted the year his grandmother died was still there. The wire fence between the pasture and the road was still there. The road itself was still there, still narrow, still empty, still turning at the same angle around the same low hill. Only the house was gone, and the family that had been in it, and the small brown dog that had barked at strangers, and the sound of his grandfather calling him in for supper at dusk, and everything, everything, everything else.

He stood a long time and looked.

He was forty-three years old. He had not been to the farm since he was seventeen. He had left in the September of his senior year to take up his uncle's offer of a room in the city, and he had never come back, not once, not even to help pack the house when his grandfather died, because by then his grandfather had been dead six weeks already and his aunt had been through the rooms and thrown away everything worth throwing away, and there had been nothing left to help with. There had been no funeral. His grandfather had left instructions that there be none. He had, according to his aunt, gone into the room at the top of the stairs and closed the door and sat down in his chair and been found three days later by the meter reader, sitting still in the chair with his hands folded on his knees and his eyes open and looking at the wall.

He had wondered, at the time, what his grandfather had been looking at.

He had wondered it many times, over the years.

He had never come back to find out.

He was here now, he told himself, because he was passing through — he was on his way to visit his mother, who lived two hours further on, in the town where he had been born — and because he had realized, driving up the interstate that morning, that he did not know what the field looked like without the house on it, and that he probably ought to know, because everyone else who had known was dead.

That was, he told himself, why he was here.

—

He walked in.

The pasture had not been mown since the sale. The grass reached his knees. He walked slowly, because he did not know where the ground would drop, and because it seemed disrespectful to walk quickly, and because he was, though he did not entirely admit it, afraid.

He walked past the foundation rectangle. He walked past the brick pile. He walked past the elm, which was larger than he remembered, its bark grown deep-furrowed in the twenty-six years since he had last laid his hand on it. He walked past the place where the vegetable garden had been, where the earth still showed the faint parallel ridges of the rows.

He was walking, he knew, toward the well.

He had not admitted this to himself in the car. He had told himself that he was going to look at the house, or the place where the house had been, and that he would stand there a moment and then get back in the car and drive on to his mother's. He had not admitted to himself that this was untrue. He had not told himself that in the seven days since his mother had called and mentioned, offhandedly, that the farm had come up in a conversation with his aunt, and that his aunt had said the well was still there, still marked by its ring of stones, in the far corner of the pasture where no one but a boy who had grown up on the land would ever think to look — he had not admitted to himself that in the seven days since that phone call, he had been unable to think of very much else.

He walked, and he thought about the well.

He remembered it in the way one remembers a small pain from childhood — sharply, unfairly, in more detail than the memory deserved. He remembered the ring of grey stones. He remembered that it was low, low enough that a small boy could lean over the top and look down. He remembered that his grandfather had held the back of his shirt the one time this had happened, that his grandfather had not spoken until the boy had wanted, on his own, to step away, and that when the boy had stepped away his grandfather had said only, in the quiet voice he used for important things, *don't shout into it.*

He remembered that he had shouted into it anyway.

He remembered that nothing had come back.

Not the echo of his own voice. Not the small rustle he would have expected from birds or leaves or the wind at the mouth of a shaft. Nothing. As if the well were not a well at all, but simply an opening in the world, and the world on the other side was very quiet, and did not answer.

He had been seven years old.

He was, now, forty-three, and he was walking across a pasture in the late afternoon of a Wednesday in September, and he was going to the well.

—

He almost missed it.

The grass had grown up around the ring, and the ring itself had settled some, and the stones were dark with lichen and rain. He almost walked past. He would have walked past, if he had not, at a particular step, felt the ground under his foot go slightly hollow — not enough to drop, but enough to warn him — and if he had not looked down and seen, half-hidden in the grass, the pale grey curve of a stone that was not the sort of stone that occurred naturally in that field.

He crouched.

He put his hand on the stone. It was cold. He pushed the grass aside.

The ring was still there. The stones were where they had been. It was smaller than he remembered — the mouth was perhaps eighty centimeters across, no more — but that was, he told himself, the mercy of childhood, which made large things larger, and the cruelty of adulthood, which shrank them again to fit an adult hand.

He knelt at the edge.

He looked in.

—

The inside of the well was black.

It was black in the way that mattered. It was not dim, and not shadowed, and not merely dark. It was black the way the inside of a closed cupboard was black — but with no walls to touch, no floor to reach, no smell of wood or dust. A darkness with no surface. He leaned closer, and his own head cast no shadow into the well, because there was nothing in the well for a shadow to fall on. His face, tilted forward, reflected nothing back at him.

He had, without meaning to, held his breath.

He let it out. He heard himself breathe. He heard his own breath in the small tiled space between his face and the mouth of the well, close and human and slightly shaking. He heard, past that, the wind in the elm at the far end of the field, moving the tips of the branches. He heard, very faintly, a car passing on the road behind him.

He did not hear anything at all from the well.

He waited.

He did not know what he was waiting for. He did not know why he had come to the well. He did not know why he had waited, for twenty-six years, to come to the well, and why he was, now, kneeling on the wet grass in his good shoes and his coat that had cost too much, waiting.

He said, softly, to the well: *hello.*

He did not know why he said it. He had told himself, walking through the pasture, that he would not speak. He would not do what he had done as a boy. He would not shout, and he would not whisper, and he would not, above all, ask anything of the well, because he had learned some things in twenty-six years, and one of them was that when a thing did not answer the first time, it was a bad idea to press it.

He said *hello* anyway.

The well did not answer.

He waited a longer moment, and then, because the waiting had become unbearable in a way he could not have described, he stood up.

He stood up too quickly. His knees hurt. He stumbled a half-step back from the ring of stones, and when he steadied himself, breathing hard, he looked down again.

The darkness in the well had risen.

It had risen by perhaps a centimeter. Not more. Not enough to spill. Not enough that he could point to it, in a photograph, and say *there, look, that is higher than it was.* It had risen the way a level of water rises in a very slow tide — quietly, patiently, in the space of a single held breath.

He stared at it.

It did not rise any further.

It sat there, level with the stones, level with the world, waiting.

He thought, quite clearly: *it heard me.*

He thought, more quietly: *it looked up.*

He did not go closer. He did not lean in again. He took two steps back, and then two more, and then he turned around, and he walked out of the pasture the way he had come — slowly, so as not to run, because he was a grown man and he would not run in a field from a hole in the ground — and he got back in his car, and he put the car in gear, and he drove away.

He did not look back until he had passed the low hill and the field was out of sight.

When he could no longer see the field, he pulled the car onto the verge, and he turned the engine off, and he sat with his hands on the wheel for a long time.

He was breathing hard.

He did not know why.

He was, he understood, going to have to come back.

chapters.title: The Line
chapters.body:
He drove on to his mother's.

He arrived late, past nine, well after the dinner she had prepared for him had gone cold on the plate she had laid on the counter with a tea-towel over it. She did not ask why he was late. She did not, in general, ask him things directly; she waited to be told, and if she was not told, she made her small assessments and drew her small conclusions and did not press. She looked at his face as he came in through the back door, and she said only, *you must be tired,* and she reheated the plate, and she sat with him at the kitchen table while he ate, and she talked to him about her neighbors and her book club and the roof that had needed repairing in the spring, and she did not ask him where he had been.

He was grateful.

He ate. He listened. He said the right things. He watched his mother's face — narrower than it had been the last time he had seen her, at Christmas, the folds of her cheeks more visible now, the eyes a little sunk — and he thought, as one thinks these things, *she is getting old,* and he thought *I will lose her,* and he thought *not yet.* And beneath these thoughts, in the quiet slow way that a second layer of thought sometimes runs beneath the first, he thought about the well.

He thought about the well while he ate. He thought about it while he helped her wash the dishes. He thought about it while he sat in the living room with her and drank the small brandy she offered him — his grandfather's brandy, which she still kept, though neither of them drank often. He thought about it lying in the small bed in the small bedroom that had been his as a boy, in the small hours when he could not sleep, and finally he thought about it standing at the window of that bedroom, looking out at the dark garden and the low fence and the moon behind a bar of cloud, and he thought:

*I am going back tomorrow.*

He thought this with the calm of a decision already made. He was mildly surprised by his own calm. He had, he realized, decided in the car, on the verge, when he had sat with his hands on the wheel and understood that he could not simply drive on. He had known, then. It had taken him only until now to admit it to himself in words.

He went back to bed. He slept for perhaps three hours, and dreamed of nothing.

—

In the morning he told his mother he had a work errand to do, and that he might be a few hours. She nodded. She said, *drive carefully,* which she had said to him every time he had left the house since he was seventeen, and he had never once heard her say it in any voice other than the one she used now, and he did not know if she meant it kindly or if it was simply the shape her mouth had learned to make.

He drove back to the farm.

The morning was cold and the air was still. A thin white fog lay along the hollows, and did not lift, even as the sun came up over the ridge. He drove slowly. The road looked different in daylight, but not by much; it was still narrow, still empty, still turned at the same angle around the same low hill. He parked in the same place he had parked the day before, on the verge outside the wall.

He got out. He took a small torch from the glove compartment. He had bought it that morning at the petrol station, along with a bottle of water and a length of clothesline from a hardware aisle that had also sold a surprising quantity of shotgun shells. He did not think he would need the clothesline. He did not know why he had bought it. He put it in his coat pocket.

He walked into the field.

—

The well was where he had left it.

He knelt at its edge. He said nothing. He did not test it. He simply looked.

The darkness inside was unchanged. It was, he saw now in the flat morning light, exactly what it had been the day before — a black without surface, a black that did not admit the day. He turned on the torch. He shone the beam down into the shaft.

The beam did not travel.

That is the only way he could have described it. The beam of light left the head of the torch and entered the mouth of the well and then it was simply gone. It did not illuminate a wall. It did not fall on distant water. It did not, as light does when it enters an ordinary shaft, scatter and lift the darkness to some vague grey suggestion of depth. It went in. It stopped. He was standing over the mouth of the well holding a torch, and the torch was on, and the light was falling in, and the light was not coming back.

He clicked the torch off. He clicked it on again. He tested the beam against the grass beside him. It made a small bright circle on the wet blades. He turned it back into the well. Nothing.

He sat back on his heels.

He thought: *this is not a well.*

He thought: *this has never been a well.*

He thought, and this thought came to him fully formed, as if it had been waiting for the words: *my grandfather knew.*

—

He drove back to the town in a strange, floating calm.

He stopped at the county records office. He asked, at the counter, whether the office kept surveys and land plats going back to the nineteenth century. The clerk — a small woman with reading glasses on a chain — said that they did, and that if he could provide the parcel number she could pull them up on the microfilm reader in the back. He gave her the parcel number. He had memorized it, he realized, from the letter his mother's brother had sent him a year ago.

She was gone a long time.

She came back with a stack of curling paper and a face that was carefully blank. She set the stack on the counter. She said, in the mild dry voice small women in reading glasses often used, *your grandfather's parcel was originally surveyed in 1863. The surveyor's notes are appended. I've marked the relevant page.*

He looked at her. She was not looking at him. She was looking at the stack of paper.

He said, *thank you.*

He took the stack to a chair in the corner and sat down and read.

—

The 1863 survey had been done in September of that year, by a man named Wren, on commission from the county to lay out the parcels that had until then been held in common by the settlers. Wren had walked the parcel in the company of a boy from the town who had known the land; his notes were terse, but detailed, and they described a rise, a stream, a wooded corner, a spring, and — in a note the clerk had marked with a small paperclip — *a pit in the southeast quarter of the northeast quarter, mouth approx. 30", of unknown depth, into which a plumb-line, weighted with 2 lbs. of lead and paid out to the full length of 200 feet, did not touch bottom. Boy remarks pit was here before his father's father. Recommend the parcel not be tilled in the SE corner within 100 yards.*

He read the note twice.

He turned the page.

There was a second note, in the same hand, written a week later. Wren had come back with a longer plumb-line — the total length was not specified, only the phrase *a length judged sufficient* — and had lowered it into the pit until his hand hurt from the paying out, and had *found no bottom, though the line was drawn tight and the weight not lifted from it.*

There was, beneath this, a smaller note in a different, older hand — a note that looked as though it had been added later by someone amending the survey — that said, simply: *see also Register of Missing Persons, 1849-1862.*

He looked up from the paper.

The clerk was watching him. She had, at some point, come out from behind the counter and was standing at the water cooler, filling a small paper cup, and she was watching him.

He said to her, softly, *did you look at that register?*

She said, *I did.*

He said, *how many?*

She said, *between 1849 and 1862, in a town of six hundred people, forty-one.*

He did not say anything.

She said, in the same mild dry voice, *the note was added in 1874, by a clerk named Ellis, who was replaced later that year for what the county minutes describe as a nervous condition. His last entry in the daybook, which we also keep, is a single line. It says, and I have copied it out from the microfilm because I have known this document since I began working here in 1979 and I have never been able to forget it, it says: '**The southeast quarter is not what we thought it was. It is not a well. It is a mouth.**'*

He looked at her.

She said, *I do not know whether this helps you or not, but you asked, and I have told you.*

He said, *thank you.*

He stood up. He gave her back the papers. He asked, before he left, whether he could photograph the two survey notes with his phone, and she said that he could, and he did, and then he thanked her again, and he went out to the car.

He sat in the car in the parking lot for a long time.

He did not photograph the note in the older hand.

He thought about it, and he decided not to.

He drove back to his mother's, and he did not tell her where he had been, and he ate the supper she had prepared, and he slept in the small bedroom of his boyhood, and he dreamed, for the first time in twenty-six years, of the well.

—

In the dream he was seven again, and his grandfather was holding the back of his shirt, and he was leaning over the ring of stones. His grandfather's hand was very steady on his shirt. His grandfather's voice was very quiet in his ear.

His grandfather said, *don't shout into it.*

He said, in the dream, *why not, grandad?*

His grandfather did not answer.

He looked up into his grandfather's face, in the dream. His grandfather was not there. There was a shape where his grandfather had been — the shape of his grandfather, tall, patient, in the checked shirt he had worn every day of the summer — but the face was wrong. The face was a small, dark, patient aperture, opening downward toward the boy, and inside the aperture was a slow turning, and inside the turning was a listening, and inside the listening was —

He woke.

He was in the small bed in the small bedroom, and his mother was standing in the doorway with a mug of tea in her hand, and she was saying, *you were shouting.*

He looked at her.

He said, *what was I saying.*

She said, *I couldn't tell. It didn't sound like words.*

She set the tea down on the bedside table. She went out. She closed the door behind her softly.

He lay in the small bed and stared at the ceiling until the tea was cold.

He was going to have to go back one more time.

chapters.title: The Answer
chapters.body:
He went in the middle of the day.

He had considered, in the small bed, going at night. He had considered going at dawn. He had considered, in the long hours before he slept again, that there might be no right time, that the well did not observe hours in the way that hours were observed by the world above. In the end he chose the middle of the day because he was, and had always been, a practical man, and because it seemed to him that if there was a moment at which the well was, so to speak, at its most quiet, it would be the moment at which the sun stood directly over it, and the field was as awake as a field could ever be.

He drove out at eleven. He arrived at the farm at eleven-thirty. He walked into the field at eleven-forty. He was at the ring of stones by ten to twelve.

He was carrying the clothesline.

He had not decided, before he left the house, what he would do with it. He had a length of nearly forty meters of white cotton line, coiled in his coat pocket, and he had a weight — a small brass sinker from a fishing tackle box in his mother's garage, of which he had stolen one, feeling absurd, while she was in the shower — and he had, in the other coat pocket, a small pair of scissors from her sewing kit. He did not know what he was going to do. He suspected he did know, but he had not admitted it to himself in words, because to admit it in words would have made it a decision, and if it was a decision he would have to defend it, and there was no one to whom he could have defended it, including himself.

He knelt at the ring of stones.

The sun was directly overhead. The field was still. He could hear a wood pigeon somewhere in the elm at the far end. He could hear, further off, the very faint hum of a tractor on some other farm. He could hear the small tickings a field makes when it is warm and dry — the small sounds of insects and seeds and the settling of the earth against itself.

He heard nothing from the well.

He tied the sinker to one end of the line. He tied it carefully, with the knot his grandfather had taught him for the same purpose, the small firm loop that would not slip. He held the weight in his palm and let the line pay out through his other hand. He lowered the weight to the mouth of the well.

He stopped.

He held the weight suspended at the lip of the darkness, and he looked at his own hand. His hand was steady. His hand was, he understood, more steady than it had any right to be. He was a man about to do a thing he did not understand for a reason he could not name, and his hand was as calm as if he were tying a shoelace.

He thought: *I am not afraid.*

He was not.

He was, he understood, something else. He was in the position of a man who has, without meaning to, arrived at the end of a long thought — a thought so long that he had lost track of when it had begun, and had noticed only, at the moment of arriving, that he had been thinking it all his life.

He lowered the weight into the well.

—

It went down easily.

He paid out the line. The sinker was small and the line was smooth, and it went down without catching, without spinning, without any of the small resistances a plumb-line ordinarily produced. He paid out five meters, and then ten, and then twenty. His arm began to tire; he switched hands. He paid out thirty. He paid out thirty-five. He reached the end of his line.

The line was slack in his hand.

He did not know what he had expected. He had expected, perhaps, to feel the small tug of the weight touching bottom, some quiet firm terminus to the exercise, the reassurance that the well was still, at its heart, a hole in the ground. Or he had expected to feel the line pull tight against the full weight of the sinker suspended, dead-drop, over some unimaginable depth. He had not expected the line to be slack. He had not expected the line to be *held.*

Because that was what it was.

He understood this with a sudden, terrible clarity. The line was not falling. The weight was not suspended. Someone — some *thing* — was holding the other end.

He held very still.

He was aware, in that moment, of an enormous quiet in the field. The wood pigeon had stopped. The tractor had stopped. The small insect tickings had stopped. He could hear his own heartbeat, close and thudding in his ears, and beyond that he could hear nothing at all — not because there was nothing to hear, but because whatever ordinarily made the sounds of a September field had, at that moment, ceased.

He waited.

He did not move. He did not draw the line up. He did not let it go. He stayed on his knees at the ring of stones, in the middle of the day, in the middle of a field, in the middle of the century, holding the very slack end of a length of white cotton line that disappeared into a mouth of darkness in the ground, and he waited.

—

The line moved.

It moved very slightly. It moved the way a line moves when the person holding the other end takes, very gently, an experimental tug. Not enough to pull it. Not enough to drag him forward. Just enough to say: *I am here. I am on this end. I know you are on that end.*

He felt the small tug, and he understood.

He understood the tug in the same way he had understood, that morning in the sun, that the well was not a well. He understood it the way a very old thing was understood — before language, before thought, before choice. The tug said, very clearly, *hello.* And it said, more quietly, *you have been here before.*

And it said, quietest of all, *you called.*

He thought: *I did not.*

Then he thought: *I did. When I was seven, I did.*

Then he thought: *I did not know I was calling.*

The tug came again. A second time. Firmer. The way a person, having said hello and received no answer, tries the door a second time — not aggressively, not unkindly, but with the gentle assumption that someone is on the other side and is, perhaps, a little slow.

He did not pull back.

He did not, he understood, know what would happen if he pulled back. He did not know what would happen if he simply let the line go. He did not know what would happen if he cut it. He had the scissors in his pocket. He had thought, in the car, that he would cut it. He had thought, in the field, walking, that he would cut it. He had thought, kneeling here, that he would cut it.

He did not cut it.

—

The tug came a third time. Longer. A slow steady pull, not quite hard enough to move him, but almost.

He felt his weight shift toward the ring of stones. The knee of his trousers pressed against the wet earth. His hand tightened on the line. He was not, he realized, holding on to keep from being pulled in. He was holding on to *keep the line in his hand.*

He was holding on because he did not want to let go.

He thought: *I have been waiting for this since I was seven.*

He thought: *I have never known this, but I have always known this.*

He thought: *my grandfather knew, and he sat in his chair at the top of the stairs and he looked at the wall, and he did not go, and now I am here, and it is my turn to decide.*

—

He knelt for a very long time.

The sun moved. He did not notice. The pigeon began, very tentatively, to call again from the elm. He did not hear it. Somewhere, at some depth in his chest, in a small quiet room he had not known was there, he felt something turning — slow, patient, unhurried — the way a very small mechanism keeps time, the way a very old thing waits for the answer to a question it has been asking for so long it has forgotten the question.

He thought about his mother. He thought about her narrow face, and her voice saying *drive carefully*, and the small bed in the small room, and the tea gone cold on the bedside table. He thought about her getting up in the morning, and coming down the stairs, and putting the kettle on, and standing at the kitchen window, and waiting for him to come home.

He thought about how she would wait.

He thought about how long she would wait before she called someone.

He thought about how she would tell the police what she knew, which would not be enough, and how she would sit in the kitchen with a strange man in a uniform asking her small careful questions, and how she would answer him carefully and quietly, and how she would not cry until after he had gone.

He thought about this.

He thought about this for a long time.

—

He drew the line up.

He drew it slowly. He drew it hand over hand, in the way his grandfather had shown him to draw a rope out of the barn well when he was a boy, patient and steady, without any sudden movement. The line came up smoothly. There was no resistance. Whatever had held it, held it no longer.

The line was thirty-five meters long. He drew it all the way up. He set it in a small coil on the grass beside him.

The sinker at the end was gone.

The line had been cut. The end was clean, and slightly frayed, in the way of something that had been snipped rather than sawn. It was, he saw when he brought it close to his face, still slightly warm.

He stared at the end of the line for a long time.

He knew that he had not cut it.

He knew, also, and this was what mattered, what the cut meant. It meant *not now.* It meant *not yet.* It meant *when you are ready, we will not need the line.*

—

He walked out of the field.

He did not run. He did not hurry. He walked as he had walked in, slowly, so as not to disturb anything, so as not to make a promise he was not prepared to keep. He got into the car. He put the car in gear. He drove away.

He drove back to his mother's. He arrived in the middle of the afternoon. She was in the garden, cutting the last of the roses. He walked around the side of the house to find her, and he stood in the doorway of the garden gate, and he watched her for a while before she noticed him — her narrow shoulders, her old cardigan, the small careful movements of her hands with the shears — and when she noticed him she straightened up and looked at him and said, only, *there you are.*

He said, *here I am.*

She said, *are you hungry?*

He said, *I am.*

She said, *come inside, then. I've made a pie.*

He went inside.

—

He did not go back to the farm.

He did not, for the rest of his life, drive past that road, or pass through that county, or speak of the field, or say his grandfather's name aloud. He did not tell his mother where he had been. He did not tell his sister when he next saw her. He did not, when he lay awake in his own bed in his own house in the city, in the small hours, and felt the very faint slow turning in his chest — the small turning he had, at first, mistaken for his own heart, and had, later, understood to be something else — he did not tell anyone about that either.

He did not need to.

He knew, and it knew, and they had reached, between them, an understanding.

He would come when he was called.

He was not, yet, called.
